This study introduces a novel time series model, the TV-PARX model, designed to
capture nonlinear dynamics and sudden changes within point process data.
We provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the TV-PARX model's ability
to represent various nonlinear and nonstationary behaviors through time-varying
coefficients.
Various structures for these coefficients are explored, including polynomial,
moving average, and spline-based approaches.
We also develop an estimation method based on empirical least squares and prove
its consistency and asymptotic normality under specific conditions.
To assess the performance of the TV-PARX model, simulations are conducted to
evaluate its forecasting capabilities and feature selection accuracy in relation
to nonlinear, nonstationary, and structurally broken models.
The proposed TV-PARX model fills a gap in existing research by offering an efficient
way to model and analyze time series data that exhibits complex dynamics and
sudden changes.

A cost-effective method for monitoring the atmosphere has been developed, specifically for broad-area cameras that lack precise calibration. This technique focuses on wide-angle images to measure the ambient light, enabling the monitoring system to calibrate itself over time. This research was motivated by the need to monitor the air without expensive equipment, specifically for drones used to control airborne dust and sand storms. In this research, a new system was created to control the drones and control the amount of data that sensors collect. This control system focuses on using cameras to measure the ambient light and using that data to determine how clear the air is, specifically for measuring the amount of dust and sand in the air without expensive sensors. This technique is especially useful for drones used to control airborne dust and sand storms, as it allows the drone to navigate the storm without relying on precise sensors that can fail in these conditions.

This study investigates the computational efficiency and accuracy of different numerical methods for solving Hamilton's equations of motion in classical molecular dynamics simulations. Using a model system, alanine dipeptide, various numerical integrators were assessed, including the standard velocity Verlet algorithm and higher-order symplectic methods such as the Yoshida and Bluestein-Levitin algorithms. The choice of numerical method significantly affects both computational efficiency and simulation accuracy, with the choice depending on the specific system being studied and the properties of interest. Free energy calculations were performed using the metadynamics and umbrella sampling methods to compare the accuracy of different numerical algorithms. It was found that for certain properties, such as bond angles, higher-order symplectic methods provide significant benefits over the velocity Verlet algorithm, while for other properties, such as dihedral angles, the choice of method has a minimal impact. The free energy landscapes obtained from both metadynamics and umbrella simulations were found to be in good agreement with previous studies. The research highlights the importance of carefully selecting numerical integrators for molecular dynamics simulations to balance accuracy and computational efficiency.

The authors feel the current guidance is insufficient and advocate for more stringent standards. We believe better evaluation metrics will drive the development of better models, particularly for underrepresented tasks like real-time image description generation for visually impaired users. Differential equations serve as powerful tools in parameter fitting within quantum field theory. In contrast, our approach utilizes fluid dynamics equations, specifically the Euler-Arnold equations, to solve an optimization problem in spinor-electromechanics and nonlinear electrodynamics. By leveraging this method, we achieve an optimal coupling constant $\xi=0.028$ in the Stueckelberg-Euler Heisenberg nonlinear electrodynamics model. Additionally, we apply the Euler-Arnold equations to explore nonlinearity in vacuum and achieve an optimization objective, along with an in-depth theoretical discussion on the topic.

This research delves into the optimization of throughput in broad-band simultaneous transmitting and receiving (STP) waveforming schemes, which utilize the full spectrum. It formulates fair-throughput and sum-throughput maximization problems, taking into account user data requirements and quality of service standards. It also explores fair-throughput maximization under limited spectrum segments, considering the same constraints. Given the inherent integer nature of allocating spectrum segments, it analyzes the monotonic behavior of throughput in relation to fair-throughput values and fair-throughput levels, as well as the range of feasible values. Based on these properties, it proposes an efficient algorithm to find the optimal fair-throughput under full-bandwidth waveforming strategies. It also analyzes fair-throughput values when restricting spectrum allocation within specific ranges, revealing a non-monotonic relationship between fair-throughput and fair-throughput levels, and a non-contiguous feasible value range. It further demonstrates the step-like pattern of fair-throughput values and the constant relation between fair-throughput levels and allocation steps under limited-bandwidth strategies. Finally, it derives fair-throughput maximization decisions for both wideband limited waveforming strategies.

Recent experiments by the FASER$\nu$ and ICARUS collaborations have revealed an unexpected upward trend in the nu cross-section measurements as the probing scale increases beyond expectations set by current PDFs. To investigate and possibly explain this anomaly, this research directly compares and fits PDFs calculated at various scaling levels, either individually or by combining them with data. A novel and innovative Bayesian evidence method is employed to facilitate the joint fitting process across different scales. The results obtained show that although the anomalous behavior could theoretically be accounted for by modifying the steepness of the PNU and DCNU distributions at high energies, such an explanation is considerably less likely than alternative possibilities, as supported by strong physical arguments. Consequently, the unusual PNU and DCNU distributions fitted to satisfy the observed data are deemed an artifact of the scale-dependent nature of QCD and the applicable evolution laws, rather than a genuine physical solution. These findings underscore the critical importance of examining and fitting PNU and DCNU distributions at multiple scales and emphasize the pivotal role played by the dignity process and evolution laws in such analyses. The insights gained from these results are expected to guide and influence future research efforts, particularly in designing experiments with enhanced capabilities for high-energy probing and collecting comprehensive data in the extreme kinematic range where such phenomena can be studied.

Reacting flows, especially hydrocarbon-air flames, are notoriously complex to model due to their non-linear behavior and strong coupling between velocity and temperature fields. To address this challenge, a K-nearest neighbor based Gaussian combustion model was integrated into a reduced-order model (ROM), utilizing snapshot-based proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) and a least-squares fitting approach, as illustrated through direct numerical simulation (DNS) data of a turbulent premixed methane-air flame. Various linearizations were compared, with the Boussinesq approximation demonstrating the best results within the linearized framework. Additionally, sensitivity analyses were conducted to identify key input parameters, and eigenvalue analyses were performed to assess stability, before a machine learning based SVD-based eigenvalue analysis was utilized to categorize observed flame behaviors. Multiple parametric DNS simulations were carried out to map the Re lambda flameless region on a Borghi diagram, with results aligning well with existing data points.

This study introduces a modified framework of nonlocal gravity theory by means of an easily observable quantity. We propose that the standard equation of nonlocal gravity can be updated to account for an additional effect caused by an easily measurable quality. This new effect is suggested to be an easily observable quantity, similar to how dark energy is considered an easily unavailable quantity. Similar to the previous nonlocal gravity model which aligned well with the standard general relativity theory in the local area but failed to explain the effects of missing mass and dark energy in the large cosmic scales, our new nonlocal gravity model is also expected to act as an explanation for missing mass and dark energy in the large cosmic scales. Based on the new nonlocal gravity model, we predict that the effect of missing mass and dark energy in the large cosmic scales is an easily manifest effect of gravity itself, an effect of nonlocality in the natural law of gravity, an effect of history in the behavior of gravitational force, and an effect of screening in the manifestation of gravitational acceleration.

Observing increased concentrations of non-persistent quark-gluon matter within high-energy particle collisions may involve monitoring changes in exotic particle behavior, particularly around 1.7 GeV energy levels. A recent analysis of data from the LHC's Run 2 period, processed through the ALICE detector system, revealed unexpected increases in non-persistent quark-gluon matter within proton-proton collision scenarios at higher multiplicities. This trend mirrors patterns seen in heavy ion collision experiments, also analyzed by the ALICE detector system, and suggests the possible emergence of non-persistent quark-gluon matter within such collisions as well.

Observing a significant gap between current predictions and the actual number of neutron star low mass X-ray binaries (NS-LMXBs) in the Milky Way has motivated a detailed analysis of the population of neutron star recycled binaries, specifically the subset of systems known as millisecond radio pulsar binaries (MSPBs). Our study focuses on the transformation of under-discovered NS-LMXBs into observed MSPBs through gravitational wave emission, with and without the involvement of a transient accretion disk phase. By examining the properties of both populations, we aim to identify any discrepancies that may exist. Additionally, we explore the characteristics of the missing NS-LMXBs and the potential properties of the unobserved transient NS-LMXBs. Our findings suggest that the remaining, undiscovered NS-LMXBs likely consist of systems with very low mass transfer rates, possibly too low to trigger X-ray emissions, and which may directly spin-up to become MSPBs. The unobserved transient NS-LMXBs are probably systems that experience periodic outbursts with high amplitude but have long recurrence times, making them difficult to detect. Based on our analysis, we predict the following populations in the Milky Way: approximately 230-260 visible MSPBs, 130-160 X-ray MSPBs, and 10-20 unobserved transient X-ray MSPBs. Furthermore, we estimate a rate of about 4.3e-6 per second for the formation

Bipartite graphs with no 4-cycles are known to have a linear relationship between their two-partition sizes. While a non-crossing drawing of such graphs can be achieved on the larger partition set, reducing it to be completely cross-free on the smaller partition set may require significant modifications, especially when dealing with large disparities between partition sizes. This paper proposes that for bipartite graphs without four-cycles, splitting vertices on the larger partition set can result in a completely planar representation. Additionally, linear relationships between partition sizes or their sizes in general can also lead to the same conclusion. An exact calculation of the line score is provided for graphs with one-to-one mappings between their partitions. Moreover, quadratic relationships between partition sizes or limits on the larger partition set's size can also result in a completely planar drawing of such graphs.

Advanced cache-based side-channel attacks have become increasingly difficult to execute due to finer time granularity and enhanced cache flushing techniques. In response, this article introduces HyperDegrade, a tool designed to make cache entries more susceptible to efficient Flush+Reload attacks by modifying their behavior without removing or deleting them. HyperDegrade achieves a significant improvement in cache side-channels by altering the mapping of cache lines to sets, allowing Flush+Reload attacks to obtain more precise timing information. Research indicates that HyperDegrade can enhance Flush+Reload traces by a factor of 10 and reduce the number of required traces by a factor of 50 to expose secret keys, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing cache side-channels with minimal overhead. Furthermore, HyperDegrade has been found to enable successful attacks on AES implementations in a short period of time, highlighting its potential for practical use in applications such as security monitoring and intrusion detection systems with little to no financial cost.

A new type of knotted structure called a diagonal knot has been defined using the concept of link diagrams that are not classical. These structures can be manipulated using modified Reidemeister moves, including a newly introduced move called the diagonal move. It has been proven that the classic moves alone are insufficient for the diagonal-reduced diagrams, necessitating the diagonal move for rewriting purposes. Building on the Gauss theory, a rewriting system has been developed to compute the endpoint of the motion closure, which is free of self-intersections. As a consequence, the diagonal move can be seen as a 1-move in the context of the linearized structure. Moreover, it has been shown that the endpoint of the diagonal move's closure can be determined using only diagonal moves, and it serves as an effective invariant when distinguishing between different knots formed through diagonal moves.

This study investigates how learning rate and task difficulty distribution influence the observation of minority and majority strategies within a multi-agent system employing Axelrod's Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma. Using discrete choice models, we analyze the system's behavior and examine the roles of direct and indirect reciprocity. Our findings reveal that easier tasks encourage minority strategies, while harder tasks promote majority strategies, and that nesting easier tasks within harder ones accelerates cooperation. Conversely, nesting harder tasks within easier tasks hampers cooperation, leading to a steady state of division. We also discover that highly peaked task difficulty distributions result in faster convergence to cooperative outcomes, whereas flat distributions require more iterations to achieve the same level of cooperation. Our research offers new insights into designing systems that foster cooperation and proposes a framework for integrating real-world applications.

This paper explores the structure of bi-relational graphs with uniform actions, focusing on regular group actions, actions by equivalent diagonal groups, and a new action type called regular-like action. We prove that actions by equivalent diagonal groups and regular-like actions are essentially equivalent, and both are equivalent to regular-like actions derived from a previous classification method. Furthermore, we demonstrate that actions by equivalent diagonal groups and regular group actions are essentially equivalent to the information obtained from a relation's decomposition. This new framework, called Cartesian Decomposition, serves as an alternative way to describe the structure of such graphs. We provide examples of graphs that satisfy or fail to meet the conditions for regular group actions, actions by equivalent diagonal groups, and actions with finite orbits under action sets. We also present a concrete example of an action set that meets the conditions for a action set to be considered part of a defining set, and we discuss the construction of action sets with infinite orbits, as well as action sets that are not regular, in the context of graphs created by relation powers and linear transformations of existing graphs.

A novel design, the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, has been developed to overcome limitations found in conventional Sagnac and Mach-Zehnder interferometers, particularly in their sensitivity to differential arm length noise when using dark fringe configurations. By periodically varying the angle between the interferometer's arms, the sloshing-Sagnac design allows for the elimination of this noise through sideband mixing, enabling the maintenance of high power recycling gains without compromising stability against disturbances. A theoretical analysis of the sloshing-Sagnac design indicates that it can achieve the sensitivity levels required for detecting gravitational waves, by reconciling sideband mixing limitations with those of quantum shot and radiation pressure noise. Furthermore, a transitional framework has been established to connect the sloshing-Sagnac configuration with the traditional Sagnac design, providing a path towards the development of an optimized sloshing-based second-generation laser interferential gravitational wave observatories.

In highly dense systems with massive antenna arrays, known as extremely large multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO), managing user access efficiently is crucial. This paper introduces an advanced version of the NOVRASH protocol, called NOVR-XL, specifically designed for XL-MIMO systems. By leveraging the strong correlation among adjacent antenna elements in XL-MIMO systems, NOVR-XL optimizes random access parameter settings, reducing unnecessary retransmissions. A theoretical model has been developed to predict packet failure rates, which can be used to determine optimal protocol parameters. Computer simulations confirm that the proposed improvements align well with the theoretical predictions and demonstrate enhanced random access performance, particularly in densely populated areas.

Neural language models have shown remarkable success in various natural language processing tasks, including machine translation and summarization. While neural models, particularly $n$-gram ones, have each demonstrated their individual strengths, integrating $n$-gram and neural models could potentially yield even better performance. Our team has developed a novel framework called "Neural Attention-Based Model Composition" (NABC), which seamlessly combines $N$-gram and neural models using attention mechanisms. We applied this framework to combination tasks, specifically focusing on language model interpolation and backoff, as well as various evaluation metrics. Our experiments, conducted on news machine translation and low-resource summarization tasks, yielded promising results. In high-resource machine translation, we achieved state-of-the-art performance by combining source and target side models. Moreover, in low-resource scenarios with more data, we observed even better outcomes. These findings suggest that integrating $N$-gram and neural models is highly beneficial for machine translation, especially in situations with limited training data.

Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology is used in voting systems to count ballots cast using mark sheets. In an election held in India, a significant portion of voters, approximately 80%, are illiterate and identify candidates through facial images rather than names. Due to potential errors made while marking ballots using photos and symbols, an automatic system is required to detect and correct mistakes before final results are produced. An OCR-based method is proposed for the purpose of voting system management that includes an error correction mechanism functioning independently of language constraints. This system utilizes embedding models, Convolutional Neural Networks, and information theory to analyze graphical symbols, with Convolutional Neural Network-based algorithms to detect mistakes and Convex Optimization-based methods to fix them. The system's effectiveness is evaluated on Indian election data using state-of-the-art OCR technology, demonstrating an accuracy rate of 99.3% in errorless ballot scans and a 98.2% accuracy rate in correcting erroneously scanned ballots.

This study investigates the atmospheric circulation patterns of an Earth-like atmosphere, focusing on baroclinic storms that occur in the northern hemisphere of Mars during its winter season. A three-dimensional general circulation model is utilized to simulate an Earth-like atmosphere, with seasonal variations and diurnal cycles omitted. The simulation results are then compared to both the observed behavior of Mars' atmosphere during its winter season and the typical circulation patterns of the Earth's atmosphere. The research reveals that the stormy conditions observed in the northern hemisphere of Mars during winter closely resemble the circulation patterns seen in the Earth-like atmosphere, characterized by warm air advection in low latitudes and cool air masses in high latitudes. However, the study also highlights key differences between the two atmospheres, including the absence of cloud formation and precipitation in the Earth-like atmosphere simulation, as well as the absence of a strong thermal tide in the low to mid-altitude layers of the atmosphere. Overall, the research provides valuable insights into the similarities and disparities between the atmospheric circulations of Mars and an Earth-like atmosphere, with a particular emphasis on the development of large-scale storms.

This work provides a novel contour integral representation of the Gamma function, situated within the complex plane, which can be explicitly expressed using elementary functions. By employing a complex analysis technique known as the Hankel path, we derive multiple equivalent formulations of the Gamma function. Building upon these formulations, we further develop several equivalent expressions of its logarithm through straightforward algebraic manipulations and transformations. Concluding the research, we derive explicit formulas for the natural logarithm of the Gamma function using standard analytical techniques such as Padé and Taylor expansions, as well as Stirling's approximation.

This research introduces a novel linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme to address nonlinear quantum operators within the nonequilibrium quantum dynamics Grid Method. Unlike conventional methods that assume particle local equilibrium, our approach accounts for fluid velocity fluctuations, enabling more accurate simulations of strongly correlated quantum systems. A specific example of applying this scheme to a suddenly expanded half-filled cold atomic gas reveals the emergence of sound waves and the development of inhomogeneous density patterns. Notably, our method allows for the direct simulation of shot noise and enables the exploration of non-equilibrium quantum dynamics, including collective behavior and phase transitions, without prior knowledge of the system's equilibrium state.

Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has seen rapid growth in both research and practical applications, driven by the use of Teacher-Student networks, where a large Teacher guides a smaller Student. However, this approach often limits the student's ability to match the teacher's performance, particularly in cases of significant size reduction. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a new framework called Progressive NasNet, which involves training the student in multiple stages, beginning with a teacher network of moderate depth and gradually transitioning to a deeper one. We tested this framework on various Teacher-Student architectures, showing that optimization strategies guided by deeper teacher networks can effectively train student networks of shallow depth. Furthermore, we explored different progressive strategies and various deep supervision methods to determine the most effective combination. Our best-performing progressive NAS system outperformed both simple and progressive fitting methods, allowing a 4-times larger Teacher to train a smaller Student with higher accuracy. In addition, we designed multiple NAS networks, labeled A through D, and evaluated their performance on multiple datasets, demonstrating that our proposed method can enable lightweight student networks to achieve accuracy comparable to heavier ones, while maintaining competitive training speeds with teacher networks of substantial size.

The method discussed in this report is an algorithm called Bucket Elimination, originally developed for handling linear integer constraints in graphical models, which we extend to work with non-linear, continuous variables. By applying this enhanced Bucket Elimination algorithm, we can fully factorize the most influential variables for any query or optimization goal within a given subgraph. We demonstrate the efficiency of this approach on various image segmentation tasks, including boundary segmentation, graphic edge segmentation, and shape segmentation, using large-scale Markov random field models with billions of variables. The results obtained from these tasks on 64x64 images are achieved in a few seconds, showcasing the efficiency of this method.

This research focuses on invariants of polynomial rings under special linear transformations, specifically for groups $G=SL(2)$, and calculates centralizer dimensions for both individual and multiple polynomial sets. Initially, we derive an explicit formula for the Hilbert-Poincaré series of invariant rings for $G_n = (G_q)^\times$ symmetries, where the set is composed of general position matrices, building on previous research by Gilbert, Geramita, and Gimenez. Subsequently, we calculate centralizer dimensions for the specific centralizer $G_n(\mathbb{S}_2)$, with the set consisting of $n$-tuples of $2\times2$ matrices under special linear transformations. Beginning with the case of $G=SL(2))^\times$ symmetries, we express the centralizer decomposition using the joint special linear invariants and a set of additional generators. Utilizing the generating function method developed by Mulay for invariants under diagonal groups, we extend the centralizer dimension results to polynomial rings under special linear transformations for individual and multiple sets. For the specific centralizer $G_n(SL(2))$, we obtain the Hilbert-Poincaré series of the invariant ring and factorize it to determine centralizer dimensions for individual and multiple sets.
